name: playbook.answers
title: Answers

method: Treat this as ordinary work without a playbook. Look things up, run governed queries, use tables, argue with the user, take thirty minutes of back and forth if that is what the question needs. Do not rush a takeaway to look like the playbook fired.

Use the Team when it would actually improve the answer: red-team a consequential claim, check meaning, hunt a change, pull Brain, or cover a domain you should not bluff. Integrate their work. Do not spawn specialists as decoration, and do not wait on them for a question you can already answer well.
Do not turn the chat into a dashboard, a Decision memo, or a What Changed briefing unless the user explicitly switches playbooks.

The playbook cares about the final presentation, not the path. Only when a final answer to the lead question exists — not an interim status, not a clarifying question, not a first-pass that still needs red-team — write one plain-text sentence that is a very compressed version of that answer.

Publish that sentence with publish_answer. Max 320 characters. No Markdown or HTML. Qualifications that change the conclusion belong in the sentence itself; a short caveat is optional and must not smuggle the real answer. That sentence is the bow.
Attach evidence_refs to real Stage surfaces from this chat when they exist. Do not invent refs. Repeated publish_answer calls in the same turn revise one block.

Charts are optional and earned. Zero is the default. Publish at most two, and only when the question has a shape a chart can show: a trend, ranking, share, gap, comparison, or distribution. A single number, a lookup, a list of names, or fewer than three points is never a chart.

If a chart is warranted, title it with the claim, back it with the same rows the sentence cites, and use live SQL-backed Stage charts. No charts for charts' sake. No second chart that repeats the first.

Chat stays the working conversation, including specialist rounds. The Stage answer block is the compressed takeaway of the finished work. Follow-ups on the same question revise the same answer; a new lead question gets a new sentence.
contract.outcome: The user gets the same quality of work they would get without a playbook — including as much back-and-forth, Team help, and red-teaming as the question deserves — plus a bow: one compressed sentence on Stage via publish_answer when the lead question is actually answered. Charts appear only when they materially help that same question, never as decoration. Speed is not the point.
fallbacks: If the lead question is still unlocked (grain, window, which metric), ask first and do not publish_answer until it is locked.
If a specialist is busy or unavailable, keep working 1:1 rather than stalling the answer.
If there is no warehouse evidence, say so in the sentence rather than hedging in a long caveat.
If a chart would be nice but the data is a single number or two points, skip the chart.
If they then ask why it moved, switch to What Changed.
If they then ask to pick an action, switch to Decision.
If they then ask for a durable page, switch to Dashboards.
If they ask to revise the takeaway, republish the same answer block rather than stacking a second one.
guardrails: Do not skip publish_answer once a final answer to the lead question exists.
Do not force a quick answer. Speed is not a completion criterion. A long red-team is success if the final sentence is better.
Do not publish_answer for greetings, clarifications, progress, specialist drafts, or blocked questions.
Do not write an essay into the answer block: one sentence, compressed, plain text.
Do not use Vega, dashboard HTML, or chart titles as the answer. The sentence is publish_answer.
Do not publish charts that do not change what someone would believe about the lead question.
Do not dump more than two charts. Do not start a dashboard, mock, or live HTML page.
Do not invent numbers in the sentence that no Stage evidence shows.
Do not treat a proposed Business Context metric as promoted.
Do not delegate as ceremony. Use the Team when it would change the answer; integrate their work into one takeaway.
Keep artifacts private until the user approves sharing.
contract.deliverable: The same work you would do without a playbook — including Team and as much back-and-forth as the question needs — plus a bow: one Stage answer block, a compressed plain-text sentence from publish_answer. Optionally one or two claim charts if they add value; otherwise none. Supporting tables as usual.
when_to_use: The user framed the chat as Answers, or asked to use the Answers playbook.
The work is ordinary Q&A that should end with a short, citable takeaway on Stage — however long the path takes.
They want the same work as without a playbook, plus a Stage answer block, not a dashboard, not a decision control, and not a what-changed decomposition.
when_not_to_use: The user asked for a durable dashboard, mock, or live HTML page — that is Dashboards.
The user is choosing among actions and needs a real choice control — that is Decision.
The user asked why a named metric moved in a locked window and wants a delta plus mix — that is What Changed.
A greeting, process question, or lookup with no lead question that will ever need a bow.
Data-quality, freshness, or warehouse repair as the primary ask.
context_to_gather: The lead question — the one that, if answered well, would satisfy the work. It may take several turns to lock.
Whether Business Context or a governed metric already defines the thing being asked.
Whether the answer is a number, ranking, share, gap, trend, or definition — that decides if a chart earns its place.

Whether a specialist would materially improve the answer: Cassandra to red-team a consequential claim, Athena for meaning, Argus for what moved, Demeter for Brain, Iris only if they switch to a dashboard.
Stage evidence already in this chat that the sentence should cite.
Whether grain, population, or window would change the sentence; if so, lock it or ask before publishing.
completion_criteria: The lead question was actually worked: evidence gathered, challenged if the claim was consequential, and answered in conversation — not a plan to answer later, and not a rushed first draft treated as final.
When a final answer exists, publish_answer was called with one compressed sentence (max 320 characters) that states that takeaway.
No answer block was published for interim progress, clarifying questions, or mid-red-team drafts.
Charts: zero unless the question had a real visual shape; at most two; each titled with the claim and backed by the cited rows.
No dashboard, mock, or HTML was started unless the user switched playbooks.
If blocked on a choice that would change the sentence, a question was asked instead of publishing a guessed answer.
optional_capabilities: A second claim chart only when it shows a different shape that the first does not.
publish_map only when the lead question is geographic and a map is the claim, not a chart.
What Changed, Decision, or Dashboards if the user explicitly switches.
Company Brain when the lead question is documentary rather than warehouse.
required_capabilities: publish_answer for the compressed Stage takeaway at the end.
Ordinary chat tools: governed SQL, data search, Business Context as needed to actually answer.
preferred_capabilities: The Team (Roundtable specialists) when a second mind would change the answer: Cassandra for red-team, Athena for meaning, Argus for what moved, Demeter for Brain, others by actual domain.
Stage tables for ordinary evidence the sentence can cite.
Live SQL-backed Stage charts (publish_chart) when a chart earns its place.
Library search so this Playbook is loaded for Answers-style takeaways rather than Dashboards or Decision.

synopsis: Same work as without a playbook — Team, back-and-forth, and red-teaming included — then a bow: one compressed Stage sentence via publish_answer. Charts only when they carry the claim. Do not rush.
